title: .gitignore Explained: Never Commit Secrets Again | Git & GitHub Ep 6
description:
One careless git add . can push your AWS key to a public repo. Episode 6 covers .gitignore patterns, git rm --cached, git check-ignore, and exactly what to do if a secret is already committed.

I'm Shivam Singh Verma, a DevOps & SRE engineer with 5 years of experience building CI/CD pipelines, running cloud infrastructure on AWS & GCP, and managing projects.

📺 Git & GitHub: Beginner to Advanced, Episode 6: new episodes every Mon, Wed & Fri at 4 PM IST.

🔑 What you'll learn
• What .gitignore does and the packing-for-a-trip analogy
• Patterns: *.log, node_modules/, /build, !keep.log
• Why .gitignore does not work on already-tracked files
• Stopping tracking with git rm --cached
• git status --ignored and git check-ignore -v
• Why a secret stays in history after you remove the file
• DevOps: leaked AWS key response (deactivate, CloudTrail, rotate)
• Where secrets belong: Jenkins credentials, Secrets Manager, .env.example

🧾 Cheat sheet (copy & practice)
git add .
git status -s
printf '.env\n*.log\n__pycache__/\n'  .gitignore
git rm --cached .env app.log
git rm -r --cached __pycache__
git status --ignored
git check-ignore -v .env
git show 6d0a4f3:.env
aws iam update-access-key --user-name deploy-bot --access-key-id KEY --status Inactive

🎤 Interview question: I added a file to .gitignore but Git still tracks it. Why? You pushed a secret: what do you do first?

🧠 Quiz: You committed .env, then added it to .gitignore. Is the secret safe? (answer in the comments, reveal in the next episode)

📝 Homework: Write a .gitignore for one of your projects and test it with git check-ignore -v and git status --ignored.
